text:
The objective is the small semi-detached tower at the lower right of the mountain's south wall, not the wall itself. Walk from camp toward the deep gully between the two and get onto the tower's own rock on the right side of that gully.

This line is the right-hand one on the tower's south face, and it has the only start on this face you can actually stand on and name: a large ledge low down, near the right side of the lowest part of the rock. Walk the base rightward until you can step up onto a ledge big enough to organise a rack on. That is the start. If you are standing on broken talus at the very bottom of the face with no ledge under you, keep walking right.

The route then confirms itself by behaviour rather than by a landmark: it zigzags. Five pitches that keep cutting back and forth across the right side of the face, which is why long slings are not optional here — rope drag is the thing people complain about, and drag is itself evidence you are on the correct line.

Negative markers. If you started at the lowest point of the face and went straight up the middle past a prominent roof, you are on the central line. If your first two pitches were a chimney or gully left of centre, you are on the three-pitch crack line further left. If you started at a pair of parallel cracks on the lower left and were off after two pitches, you are on the short cracks.

Also worth knowing: this route's descent is not the mountain's summit walk-off. It comes off the tower by the north-east gully in three rappels of about seventy-five feet, each covered by a doubled sixty-metre rope. If somebody has told you to walk west off the summit, they were describing the mountain, not the tower.

text: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 23 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: The Monk is a distinct, smaller detached tower/buttress leaning against Cathedral Peak's south/east flank, not part of the main South Face wall. From Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the same talus slope toward Cathedral Pass but hike up into the deep gully separating Cathedral Peak from The Monk, then start on The Monk's own faces (right side of the gully); most Monk routes descend via rappels down the NE gully.

text:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east about 12 miles to the WSDOT Shuksan maintenance facility and turn onto Twin Lakes Road (FS-3065). The first 4.5 miles to the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead are passenger-car friendly; beyond that the road narrows and is not maintained for passenger vehicles, and high-clearance is recommended for the final two miles to Twin Lakes. If the upper road is out, park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and add roughly four miles round trip and 1,500 ft of gain.

From the isthmus between the Twin Lakes take the High Pass Trail — about two miles, losing roughly 300 ft as it skirts below Winchester Mountain before climbing to the pass.

From High Pass, ascend the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's South Arm; there is a trail here in summer. From the col descend slightly and traverse the basin.

The Pleiades are a series of jagged spires on Larrabee's east ridge, so this is not one summit but several.

edits.new: Starting from High Pass, go up the NNE scree or snow slope to the col in

text: The climb starts at a gully leading to the notch between the first and second Pleiades, and finding it is a three-step sequence from High Pass. Up the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's south arm. Down slightly from the col. Across the basin. Then up the gully to the notch. The descent in the middle is the step people skip, and skipping it puts you on Larrabee's south ridge instead. The notch is between two spires and that is the confirmation. You are not aiming for a summit, you are aiming for the gap between the first and second towers of a jagged row. Arriving somewhere with rock on both sides of you and the basin below is the arrival. From the notch the two peaks are very different, and the choice matters. The second peak, to the east, is an easy scramble. The first peak, to the west, is third class in summer and has been reported as a snowy knife-edge with slabby, high-consequence exposure in winter conditions. Going the wrong way out of the notch is the difference between a walk and a serious ridge. What being on the wrong objective looks like: Larrabee's own South Ridge route leaves the same basin and its base is two parallel channels about 30 ft apart on a southwest spur at 6,900 ft — take the right-hand one for Larrabee. American Border Peak's route contours much further north around Larrabee's west flank to a col at 6,200-6,300 ft. All three leave High Pass. Only this one crosses the basin under Larrabee's east-side spires. The rock is loose and sandy throughout, which makes downclimbing as hazardous as the climb up. Keep the party close so nobody is under a falling stone.

edits.new: Climb the NNE scree or snow slope to the col in Larrabee's south arm.

text: The Scoop follows a striking line of finger-and-hand cracks up to 1,000 ft to the right of the West Face and the Tempest, named for its crux pitch, which resembles a giant ice-cream scoop. Established by Matt Clifton, Evan Cabodi, and Stewart Matthiesen on August 9, 2010, after significant lichen-cleaning. It's considered one of the best 5.11 hand-and-finger cracks in the Pacific Northwest; a bypass exists via a 5.10+ hand crack ("Nectar") to the right for parties wanting to skip the 5.11c crux.

text: P1 (5.9, ~100 ft): bouldery move off the ground to easier terrain, belay below a small rotting tree. P2 (5.10a, ~100 ft): move into a groove, tough moves out right where climbing eases. P3 (5.10a, ~100 ft): fun climbing into a dihedral crux, short slab to 'Launch Ledge'; move the belay left ~30 ft before P4. P4 (5.11c, ~195 ft, 'The Scoop'): nice crack into a corner, sustained finger/hand jams up and left, finishing with a 5.10 hand crack to a nice belay ledge (a 5.10+ variation, 'Nectar', skips the crux via a hand crack to the right). P5 (5.10b, ~100 ft): down and left on a small ledge into a slab dihedral (small cams/nuts useful, wet early season), out left of a roof to a belay ledge. P6 (5.10a, ~100 ft): right side up, back left to a rock tooth, a nice 5.9 dihedral to a small roof and final ledge (tree belay). P7-10: easy fifth-class climbing up and left to the summit and the balanced rock.

text: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~8.5 miles from Leavenworth) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599). The first 1.5 miles climb gently through forest alongside Mountaineer Creek to a log-bridge crossing; about a mile past that, fork left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A). The final push switchbacks up a boulder moraine to the Colchuck Lake outlet — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, 2.5-3 hours at a steady pace. This is the last reliable water; fill up here. Work around toward the lake's south/east side and pick up the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, following it up steep talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; this slope holds snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history). Break off climber's-left through a band of dense slide alder and heather — the brushy crux of the hike-in, 15-20 minutes — to the base of the gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock's main wall. The Tempest begins at the center of the face, below the long bulge/roof, roughly mid-way along the base — a bit right of the West Face's gully start. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final approach scramble; many parties rope up. Total trailhead-to-base time runs 3.5-4 hours.

text: Immediately past the creek, leave the trail on a cairned climbers' path along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch into Temple Canyon. Where the talus narrows to about 75 ft, work right onto a class 2-3 ledge system beside a waterfall, then up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose path climbs Temple Canyon near the stream, the last reliable water. Near the head of the canyon scramble up and left onto the larch plateau of Tamarack Meadows, about 6,600 ft, cross the talus and boulder field above it, and find the sandy ramp under an overhang at the far right-hand end of the base of the ridge.

text: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead on Icicle Creek Road (about 4.2 mi from US-2, ~1,300 ft elevation), cross Icicle Creek on the trail bridge and begin the long, switchbacking climb up open, sun-baked slabs on Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553 — this lower stretch is notoriously hot with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels necessary for the first few miles. The grade eases as the trail enters the hanging valley and reaches Nada Lake at roughly 5.5-5.6 miles (~5,000 ft), banking most of the day's approach mileage but only a bit over half the total gain. Follow the trail/use path along the lake's west shore past scattered campsites to Nada Creek near the lake's upper end — a boulder-hop in normal summer flow, but a genuine ford in early-season high water. Immediately past the creek, leave the maintained trail: climb a cairned climbers' path staying along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch that opens into Temple Canyon. Where the talus narrows to roughly 75 ft, work right onto a class 2-3 ledge system that skirts a waterfall, then continue up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose dirt-and-rock climbers' path then leads into Temple Canyon proper, staying near the stream (the last reliable water before the summit block) as it steepens toward the canyon head. Near the top, scramble up and left onto the broad, larch-dotted plateau of Tamarack Meadows (~6,600 ft), cross another talus/boulder field above treeline, and follow a final sandy ramp under an overhang to the base of the South Ridge's technical section. Figure roughly 8 miles and ~7,000 ft one-way from the trailhead to the 8,295 ft summit — about 16-16.5 miles round trip, a very long car-to-car day if not camping at Nada Lake or in the canyon. Hazards: sustained sun exposure with no shade on the lower switchbacks, an unbridged Nada Creek crossing that gets serious with early-season snowmelt, faint cairn-dependent route-finding above Nada Lake, loose talus and scree throughout Temple Canyon, and lingering snow on north-facing ledges into early summer.

The lower Snow Lakes trail switchbacks up open, sun-baked slabs with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels sensible; the grade eases into the hanging valley at Nada Lake around five and a half miles. text: From the gully scramble (as per West Face), from the sandy ledge climb 10 ft of 5.7 and step left to a small ledge below a left-facing corner with a bolt about 8 ft up. P1 (20m, 5.11, 1 bolt): the corner to a 2-bolt ledge belay. P2 (20m, 5.11, 5 bolts): traverse left past bolts and knobs, layback past 3 bolts to a 2-bolt belay. P3 (40m, 5.11+, 3 bolts): up a seam, an insecure crux to the 'flower power' crack, then a steeper corner to the 'Sky Lounge' ledge (2 bolts). P4 (45m, 5.12, 8 bolts): traverse right, up a featured slab (5.10), through a power flare on tips-to-fingers crack to a roof, traverse left under the roof, stem past a bolt (avoiding a big flake) to a 2-bolt anchor in an alcove — the last rappel point on the route. P5 (30m, 5.11-, no bolts): small roof to a long hand/finger crack, trending right to a sandy alcove belay (shared with Let It Burn's P6/7 stance). P6+: finishes per Let It Burn to the summit.

text: Climb starts at the saddle atop Pineapple Pass (the notch between The Tooth and the smaller pinnacle just south of it). Four pitches of low-5th-class climbing (a short 4th-class section included) wind up ledges and flakes to the summit; the crux 4th pitch has multiple options from juggy 5.4 flakes to a steeper 5.8 crack for those seeking harder climbing. Expect crowds, some loose rock, and outstanding summit views of the Stuart Range, Chair/Snoqualmie Mountain, and Mount Rainier.

text: Climbed by Sam Boyce and Kyle Willis in July 2018 as part of a four-day 'Boston Marathon' link-up; they knew of no previously published complete west-to-east crossing. From Sibley Pass, a faint climbers' trail (generally used to access Marble Creek Basin) leads along the ridge; the route then tags West, Middle, and East Triad in sequence along the crest. The west face of Middle Triad has the best rock on the route and holds the technical crux at 5.6 R; elsewhere the ridge is serious, exposed 4th-class and low-5th-class scrambling on generally poor ('choss') rock. A separate 2018 descent of the East Ridge toward the Eldorado Glacier involved pushing past large loose blocks and roughly 500 ft of very exposed 5.6–5.7 downclimbing to reach the glacier.
